title: HEAT AND TEMPERATURE — Chapter 9, Class 11 Physics (Concepts, All 5 Scales & Step-by-Step Numericals)
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Temperature vs Heat | Effects of Heat | Thermal Equilibrium & Zeroth Law | Thermometry | The 5 Temperature Scales & Fundamental Interval | General Conversion Formula | Numericals (Direct Conversion, Coincidence/Double-Reading Problems, Faulty Thermometer Problems, Arbitrary/Offset Scale Problems, Rate/Error Problems)

🌡️ TEMPERATURE — DEFINITION: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of all molecules present in a body. It tells you the DIRECTION heat will flow (hot → cold). Measured using a thermometer. SI unit: kelvin (K).

🔥 HEAT — DEFINITION: Heat is the SUM (total) of the kinetic energy of all molecules of a substance. It is a form of energy, measured in joules. Heat flows from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until equilibrium is reached.

💡 KEY CONCEPTUAL DIFFERENCE (exam favorite): Temperature is an AVERAGE (intensive property — doesn't depend on amount of substance). Heat is a TOTAL/SUM (extensive property — depends on mass/amount). This is why a bucket of lukewarm water can contain MORE heat than a cup of boiling tea, even though its temperature is lower — more molecules means a bigger total, even if each molecule individually has less average energy.

⚡ EFFECTS OF HEAT: When heat is applied to a body, it can bring: (i) Change in temperature (ii) Change in volume (iii) Change of state of matter (iv) Electric effect (v) Generation of light energy (vi) Change in resistance.
⚖️ THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when NO heat flows from one to the other after being brought into contact — meaning they are at the same temperature.

📐 ZEROTH LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. (This law is what actually justifies using a thermometer — the thermometer is the 'third system'.)
🧪 THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM: A system that can be described using thermodynamic parameters — Temperature, Pressure, Volume, and Heat exchange.
🔬 THERMOMETRY: The science of temperature and its measurement. THREE MAIN STEPS: (i) Construction (ii) Calibration (iii) Sensitiveness.
═══════════ SECTION A: THE 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES & FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL ═══════════

💡 WHAT IS 'FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL'? It is simply the NUMBER OF DIVISIONS between the Lower Fixed Point (LFP — ice/melting point) and Upper Fixed Point (UFP — steam/boiling point) on a scale. This single number is the KEY to comparing any two scales, because it tells you how 'coarse' or 'fine' each degree-step is. A bigger fundamental interval = smaller, finer degree-steps.
📝 TABLE A1 — ALL 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES

| Scale | Symbol | LFP (Ice Point) | UFP (Steam Point) | Fundamental Interval (UFP−LFP) | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Celsius | °C | 0 | 100 | 100 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Fahrenheit | °F | 32 | 212 | 180 | Relative (0 ≠ ice point) |
| Kelvin | K | 273 | 373 | 100 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |
| Réaumur | °R (Ré) | 0 | 80 | 80 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Rankine | °Ra | 491.67 | 671.67 | 180 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |

🔑 FEEL IT, DON'T MEMORIZE: Kelvin is just Celsius SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Celsius, fundamental interval 100). Rankine is just Fahrenheit SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Fahrenheit, fundamental interval 180). So Celsius↔Kelvin is a pure SHIFT (add 273), and Fahrenheit↔Rankine is also a pure SHIFT (add 459.67). But Celsius↔Fahrenheit needs both a SHIFT and a SCALE change (×9/5) because their degree-sizes differ.

📐 GENERAL CONVERSION FORMULA (works for ANY two scales, including Rankine): (Reading − LFP)/(Fundamental Interval) is the SAME fraction on every scale, because all scales measure the identical physical range between ice point and steam point.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Students often try converting Rankine using the Celsius-style formula (Ra−0)/x. WRONG — Rankine's zero is absolute zero, NOT the ice point, so you MUST use (Ra−491.67)/180, matching Fahrenheit's fundamental interval of 180, not Kelvin's 100.
═══════════ SECTION B: DIRECT CONVERSION NUMERICALS ═══════════
📝 NUMERICAL B1: Convert 30°C into Fahrenheit scale.
Step 2: Substitute C = 30: 30/100 = (F−32)/180
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 30×180/100 = F−32 → 54 = F−32
✅ ANSWER: 30°C = 86°F
📝 NUMERICAL B2: Convert 98.6°F (normal body temperature) into Kelvin and Rankine.
Step 2: Convert to Kelvin: K = C+273 = 37+273 = 310 K
Step 3: Convert to Rankine directly from Fahrenheit: Ra = F+459.67 = 98.6+459.67 = 558.27

💡 TIP: Kelvin was obtained from Celsius by pure ADDITION (+273), Rankine from Fahrenheit by pure ADDITION (+459.67) — no multiplication needed, since each absolute scale shares its degree-size with its 'parent' relative scale.
═══════════ SECTION C: 'DOUBLE READING' & 'COINCIDING SCALE' NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: These problems give a RELATIONSHIP between two scale readings (e.g. 'one is double the other' or 'both are equal') instead of a direct value. Assign a variable to the unknown common temperature, express both readings in terms of it using the given relationship, plug into the master equation, and solve.
📝 NUMERICAL C1: At what temperature will the Kelvin reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let K = 2F
✅ ANSWER: At 176.69°F (353.38 K), Kelvin reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C2: At what temperature will the Celsius reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let F = x, so C = 2x
✅ ANSWER: At −12.307°F, Celsius reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C3: At what point does the Kelvin reading coincide with (equal) the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let both = x
✅ ANSWER: At 574.25 K = 574.25°F, the readings coincide.
📝 NUMERICAL C4 (Concept-challenging — physically impossible case): At what temperature would the Rankine reading equal the Celsius reading numerically?
Step 1: Let both = x. Using Ra = 1.8(C+273): x = 1.8(x+273)
Step 3: Check against absolute zero (−273°C): −614.25°C is colder than absolute zero, so it cannot exist.
✅ ANSWER: No physically valid solution — the equality would require a temperature below absolute zero.
💡 TIP: ALWAYS sanity-check your final answer against absolute zero (−273°C / 0 K) when an absolute scale is involved — algebra can give you a number, but physics can reject it.
📝 NUMERICAL C5: At what temperature will the Réaumur reading be numerically equal to the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let both = x. x/80 = (x−32)/180
✅ ANSWER: At −25.6°Ré = −25.6°F, the readings coincide.
═══════════ SECTION D: FAULTY / MISCALIBRATED THERMOMETER NUMERICALS ═══════════

📐 METHOD: A faulty thermometer has WRONG numbers marked at its LFP and UFP, but still divides the space between them proportionally. Use: (Faulty reading − Faulty LFP)/(Faulty UFP − Faulty LFP) = (Correct reading − Correct LFP)/(Correct UFP − Correct LFP)
📝 NUMERICAL D1: A faulty thermometer has fixed points marked at 2 and 98 (instead of 0 and 100). What is the correct Celsius temperature when it reads 20°C?
✅ ANSWER: 18.75°C.
📝 NUMERICAL D2: A thermometer reads the melting point of ice as −10°C, and reads 60°C in place of the correct 50°C. Find its reading at the actual boiling point of water (100°C).
✅ ANSWER: The faulty thermometer reads 130°C at the true boiling point.
📝 NUMERICAL D3: The distance between LFP and UFP on a thermometer is 80 cm. Find the Celsius temperature when mercury has risen 10.4 cm above the LFP.
Step 1: 80 cm = 100°C, so 1 cm = 100/80 parts
✅ ANSWER: 13°C.
💡 TIP: This is the same ratio logic as the faulty-thermometer formula — physical stem length is just another 'scale' being converted into Celsius.
═══════════ SECTION E: ARBITRARY / OFFSET SCALE NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) ═══════════
📐 METHOD: These invent a new scale with its own LFP/UFP. Treat it exactly like Celsius vs Fahrenheit — set up the ratio, don't panic just because the scale is unfamiliar.
📝 NUMERICAL E1: In an arbitrary scale, water freezes at 40° and boils at 290°. Find the reading on this scale corresponding to 62°C.
Step 1: Arbitrary fundamental interval = 290−40 = 250
✅ ANSWER: 62°C corresponds to 195° on the arbitrary scale.
📝 NUMERICAL E2: A new scale 'X' has its ice point at −20°X and steam point at 130°X. Find the reading on X when Celsius reads 50°C.
Step 1: Fundamental interval of X = 130−(−20) = 150
✅ ANSWER: X = 55°X
📝 NUMERICAL E3 (two unknown scales, no Celsius needed): Thermometer P has LFP=10, UFP=160. Thermometer Q has LFP=20, UFP=120. When P reads 70, what does Q read?
✅ ANSWER: Q reads 60.
💡 TIP: Celsius is not mandatory as a 'bridge' — the ratio method works between ANY two linear scales directly.
📝 NUMERICAL E4: Scale 'Y' has the SAME fundamental interval as Celsius (100 divisions) but its ice point is marked at 50°Y. If Y reads 68°Y, find the Celsius equivalent.
Step 1: Equal fundamental intervals → pure shift relationship: C = Y−50
✅ ANSWER: 18°C.

💡 TIP: When two scales share the SAME fundamental interval, conversion is always pure addition/subtraction (like Celsius↔Kelvin) — no multiplication needed. Different fundamental intervals force a scaling step.
═══════════ SECTION F: RATE / ERROR / CHANGE NUMERICALS ═══════════
📝 NUMERICAL F1: A Fahrenheit thermometer reads 99°F when a standard Celsius thermometer reads 37°C. Find the error in the Fahrenheit scale.
Step 1: True Fahrenheit equivalent of 37°C: 37/100 = (F−32)/180 → 6660 = 100F−3200 → F = 98.6
✅ ANSWER: 0.4°F.
📝 NUMERICAL F2: A lab thermometer reads only in °F. Initial sample temperature is 68.2°F, and it must be increased by 40°C. Find the final temperature in °F.
Step 1: For a CHANGE (not absolute reading), use only the scaling ratio: 100 parts in °C = 180 parts in °F
Step 2: 40°C change = (180/100)×40 = 72°F change
✅ ANSWER: 140.2°F.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Never apply the full C-to-F formula (×9/5, +32) to a temperature CHANGE — the '+32' offset applies only to absolute readings. For a change, only the scaling factor (180/100) applies. This is the single most common error in this topic.
📝 NUMERICAL F3: A Celsius scale reads 30°C when a standard Kelvin scale reads 300 K. Find the error in the Celsius reading.
Step 1: True Celsius equivalent of 300 K: C = 300−273 = 27
Step 2: Error = 30−27 = 3
✅ ANSWER: 3°C.
📝 NUMERICAL F4: What are the temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit when 2/3 of the Fahrenheit reading equals 1/2 of the Celsius reading?
📝 NUMERICAL F5 (Rankine, concept-challenging): A gas thermometer shows a temperature change from 500°Ra to 680°Ra. Express this change in Celsius degrees.
Step 1: Rankine change = 680−500 = 180 Ra
Step 2: Since Rankine shares fundamental interval 180 with Fahrenheit, and Fahrenheit-to-Celsius scaling ratio is 100/180: Celsius change = 180×(100/180) = 100
✅ ANSWER: A 180°Ra change equals a 100°C change.

💡 TIP: This confirms the 'feel': Rankine degree-size = Fahrenheit degree-size, so converting a Rankine CHANGE to Celsius always goes through the F→C scaling ratio (100/180), never through the absolute-zero offset (491.67), since offsets cancel out in a difference.

🎯 QUICK SUMMARY OF ALL METHODS: (1) DIRECT CONVERSION between named scales → plug into the master equation (C−0)/100=(F−32)/180=(K−273)/100=(Ré−0)/80=(Ra−491.67)/180. (2) 'DOUBLE' or 'COINCIDE' problems → assign one variable to the unknown temperature, express both readings in terms of it, substitute into the master equation, and sanity-check against absolute zero. (3) FAULTY THERMOMETER problems → use (Faulty−FaultyLFP)/(FaultyUFP−FaultyLFP) = (Correct−CorrectLFP)/(CorrectUFP−CorrectLFP). (4) ARBITRARY/OFFSET SCALES → same ratio method; Celsius is not mandatory as a bridge. (5) CHANGE/DIFFERENCE in temperature → apply ONLY the scaling ratio between fundamental intervals, NEVER the additive offset.
